transitivity: both — transitive (change the date), intransitive (the weather changed)
gloss: To become different, or to make something different.
examples: Nothing will *change* unless somebody asks.
She *changed* her mind at the last minute.
The neighborhood has *changed* a lot in ten years.

gloss: To change something, usually in a small or partial way.
examples: We may have to *alter* the schedule.
The tailor *altered* the sleeves for free.
Nothing had been *altered* in the original file.
contrast: *Alter* (change) sounds exactly like *altar* (the table in a church), but only *alter* is a verb.

gloss: To change part of something to make it better or more suitable.
examples: You can *modify* the settings later.
They *modified* the design after the first tests.
We are *modifying* the contract to add a clause.
contrast: -y after a consonant becomes -ie-: *modifies*, *modified* — but *modifying* keeps the y.

transitivity: both — transitive (adjust the volume), intransitive (adjust to a new city)
gloss: To change something slightly, or to get used to a new situation.
examples: *Adjust* the mirror before you drive.
He *adjusted* quickly to the new schedule.
She is still *adjusting* to life in a big city.
contrast: In the sense of getting used to something, *adjust* takes **to**: *adjust to the cold*.

transitivity: both — transitive (transform a room), intransitive (the neighborhood transformed)
gloss: To change something completely, usually for the better.
examples: A coat of paint can *transform* a room.
The company *transformed* itself in five years.
The old factory is being *transformed* into apartments.
contrast: *Transform* something **into** something else.

transitivity: both — transitive (convert a garage), intransitive (the sofa converts into a bed)
gloss: To change something into a different form, purpose, or system.
examples: They want to *convert* the garage into an office.
He *converted* the money at the airport.
The barn has been *converted* into a studio.
contrast: Verb: kuhn-VURT. The noun (someone who changed religion) is KAHN-vurt.

transitivity: both — transitive (switch seats), intransitive (switch to a new plan)
gloss: To change from one thing to another, or to exchange one thing for another.
examples: Let's *switch* seats so you can see.
She *switched* to a cheaper phone plan last month.
He keeps *switching* between two browsers.
contrast: The third person adds -es after -ch: *switches*.

transitivity: both — transitive (shift the meeting), intransitive (opinion shifted)
gloss: To move or change position, direction, or emphasis.
examples: Public opinion can *shift* very quickly.
We *shifted* the meeting to Thursday.
The wind has *shifted* to the north.

gloss: To change a text, plan, or figure after looking at it again.
examples: I need to *revise* my estimate.
The editor *revised* the opening paragraph.
They have *revised* the forecast twice this year.
contrast: In American English *revise* means to change a text. The British use of *revise* for exam study is not American.

gloss: To change a law, document, or statement slightly in order to improve it.
examples: Congress may *amend* the bill next week.
We *amended* the agreement to include travel costs.
The rules were *amended* last spring.

gloss: To make a small change to something in order to improve it.
examples: Let me *tweak* the color a little.
He *tweaked* the recipe and it came out better.
They are *tweaking* the app before the launch.

ru: менять на противоположное, отменять, полностью изменить
transitivity: both — transitive (reverse a decision), intransitive (the trend reversed)
gloss: To change something to its opposite, or to undo it.
examples: The court could *reverse* the decision.
They *reversed* the order of the two chapters.
The trend has *reversed* since January.

transitivity: both — transitive (transition the team to new software), intransitive (he transitioned to a new career)
gloss: To move or change from one state, system, or job to another.
examples: The company plans to *transition* to solar power.
She *transitioned* from teaching to software work.
We are *transitioning* to the new system in March.
contrast: *Transition* takes **to** or **into**: *transition to remote work*.

gloss: To develop gradually into a different or more advanced form.
examples: Languages *evolve* whether we like it or not.
The project *evolved* into something much bigger.
Their style has *evolved* over the years.
contrast: *Evolve* **into** something new.

gloss: To change the form or structure of something significantly.
examples: New rules could *reshape* the whole industry.
The storm *reshaped* the coastline.
Technology is *reshaping* how we work.

transitivity: both — transitive (modernize a kitchen), intransitive (the industry has modernized)
gloss: To make something more modern by adding new methods or equipment.
examples: The city wants to *modernize* its buses.
They *modernized* the kitchen last year.
The airport is being *modernized* in stages.
contrast: American spelling is *modernize*; British writing often has *modernise*.

gloss: To change and improve the form or appearance of something.
examples: They plan to *revamp* the website.
The menu was *revamped* over the summer.
We are *revamping* the training program.

gloss: To change or repair something thoroughly, from top to bottom.
examples: The state may *overhaul* its tax code.
They *overhauled* the engine last winter.
The whole system is being *overhauled*.
contrast: Verb: oh-vur-HAWL. The noun (a complete repair) is OH-vur-hawl.

transitivity: both — transitive (reform the system), intransitive (he has reformed)
gloss: To change an institution or a person's behavior in order to improve it.
examples: Both parties promised to *reform* the system.
The prison was *reformed* after the report came out.
He *reformed* his eating habits at fifty.
contrast: *Reform* (rih-FORM) means improve; *re-form* with a hyphen (ree-FORM) means form again.

gloss: To organize something in a new way, especially a company or a debt.
examples: The bank offered to *restructure* the loan.
They *restructured* the department last fall.
The company is *restructuring* again.

transitivity: both — transitive (reorganize the files), intransitive (the company reorganized)
gloss: To arrange something in a new and usually better way.
examples: We should *reorganize* the files by year.
She *reorganized* the whole closet in one afternoon.
The team is being *reorganized* under new management.

gloss: To change the position or the order of things.
examples: Can we *rearrange* the chairs?
He *rearranged* the furniture while I was out.
I am *rearranging* my schedule to make room for it.

gloss: To put a new thing or person in the place of another.
examples: We need to *replace* the batteries.
A younger manager *replaced* him in June.
The windows have been *replaced* twice.
contrast: *Replace* X **with** Y — never *replace X on Y*.

gloss: To give one thing and get another in exchange.
examples: Do you want to *swap* seats?
They *swapped* phone numbers after class.
We ended up *swapping* stories all night.
contrast: One vowel plus one final consonant doubles: *swapped*, *swapping*.

gloss: To extend the period of something official, or to make something fresh again.
examples: I have to *renew* my passport this month.
She *renewed* the lease for another year.
The membership has been *renewed* automatically.
contrast: American pronunciation is rih-NOO, not rih-NYOO.

gloss: To bring something back to its original condition, or to give it back.
examples: They plan to *restore* the old theater.
Power was *restored* around midnight.
The museum is *restoring* the painting.

gloss: To make something more current by adding the newest information.
examples: Please *update* the spreadsheet before Friday.
He *updated* us right after the call.
The app has been *updated* three times this week.
contrast: Verb: up-DAYT. The noun (a new version, a piece of news) is UP-dayt.

gloss: To replace something with a better or newer version.
examples: It may be cheaper to *upgrade* than to buy a new one.
They *upgraded* us to a bigger room.
We are *upgrading* the servers this weekend.
contrast: Verb: up-GRAYD. The noun is UP-grayd.

transitivity: both — transitive (refresh the page), intransitive (the page refreshes on its own)
gloss: To make something new, current, or lively again.
examples: *Refresh* the page and try again.
A short nap *refreshed* him completely.
The screen has been *refreshing* every thirty seconds.
contrast: The third person adds -es after -sh: *refreshes*.

ru: перерабатывать, сдавать на переработку; использовать заново
transitivity: both — transitive (recycle bottles), intransitive (this town recycles)

examples: We *recycle* paper and glass every week.
The bottles were *recycled* into fleece jackets.
The city has been *recycling* food waste since 2019.

transitivity: both — transitive (increase the price), intransitive (prices increased)
gloss: To become larger in number, amount, or degree, or to make something larger.

The company *increased* wages by four percent.
Traffic has been *increasing* all year.

transitivity: both — transitive (expand the parking lot), intransitive (metal expands)
gloss: To become larger, or to make something cover more space.
examples: They hope to *expand* into Canada next year.
The metal *expanded* in the heat.
We are *expanding* the parking lot.

transitivity: both — transitive (extend a deadline), intransitive (the trail extends for miles)
gloss: To make something longer in time or distance, or to reach over an area.
examples: Can you *extend* the deadline by a week?
They *extended* my visa by three months.
The trail has been *extended* all the way to the lake.

gloss: To make something bigger in size.
examples: We can *enlarge* the photo for the frame.
The shop *enlarged* its selection of bikes.
The waiting room is being *enlarged*.

gloss: To lift something, to increase an amount, or to bring up a child.

They *raised* almost ten thousand dollars.
She has *raised* three kids on her own.
contrast: *Raise* is regular and always takes an object (*raise prices*); *rise* is irregular and never takes one (*prices rose*).

gloss: To increase or improve something, often quickly.
examples: A discount might *boost* sales.
The coach's speech *boosted* everyone's confidence.
They are *boosting* production before the holidays.

transitivity: both — transitive (multiply six by four), intransitive (the problems multiplied)
gloss: To increase greatly in number, or to add a number to itself a given number of times.
examples: Problems tend to *multiply* when you ignore them.
The number of stores *multiplied* in two years.
Rumors were *multiplying* by the hour.
contrast: -y becomes -ie-: *multiplies*, *multiplied*; but *multiplying* keeps the y.

transitivity: both — transitive (double the recipe), intransitive (prices doubled)
gloss: To become twice as much, or to make something twice as much.
examples: The rent could *double* in five years.
We *doubled* the recipe for the party.
Sales have *doubled* since April.

transitivity: both — transitive (triple the order), intransitive (costs tripled)
gloss: To become three times as much, or to make something three times as much.
examples: Our costs could *triple* next year.
The town *tripled* in size after the factory opened.
Orders have *tripled* since the review came out.

ru: обостряться, нарастать; обострять, передавать на верх
transitivity: both — transitive (escalate the issue to a manager), intransitive (the argument escalated)
gloss: To become more serious or more intense, or to make something so.
examples: A small argument can *escalate* fast.
The dispute *escalated* into a strike.
Costs have been *escalating* all year.

transitivity: both — transitive (intensify the search), intransitive (the storm intensified)
gloss: To become stronger or more extreme, or to make something so.

The pain *intensified* after an hour.

gloss: To collect or increase gradually over time.
examples: Dust will *accumulate* in a week.
He *accumulated* a lot of debt in college.
Snow was *accumulating* on the front steps.

transitivity: both — transitive (deepen the channel), intransitive (the crisis deepened)
gloss: To become deeper or stronger, or to make something so.
examples: Silence can *deepen* a misunderstanding.
The crisis *deepened* over the winter.
Their friendship has *deepened* since the trip.

transitivity: both — transitive (widen the road), intransitive (the gap widened)
gloss: To become wider, or to make something wider or larger in scope.
examples: The city plans to *widen* the road.
The gap between the two teams *widened*.
They are *widening* the search to other states.

transitivity: both — transitive (broaden the program), intransitive (his tastes broadened)
gloss: To increase the range of something, or to become wider in range.
examples: Travel can *broaden* your view of the world.
The course *broadened* my interests.
They are *broadening* the program to include teenagers.

transitivity: both — transitive (lengthen a dress), intransitive (the days lengthen)
gloss: To become longer, or to make something longer.
examples: We can *lengthen* the curtains a few inches.
The days *lengthened* through April.
The line was *lengthening* by the minute.

transitivity: both — transitive (heighten the tension), intransitive (tension heightened)
gloss: To make a feeling or an effect stronger, or to become stronger.
examples: Music can *heighten* the tension in a scene.
The delay *heightened* everyone's worry.
Security has been *heightened* at the airport.
contrast: The *gh* is silent: HY-tuhn.

transitivity: both — transitive (strengthen a wall), intransitive (the storm strengthened)
gloss: To become stronger, or to make something stronger.
examples: These exercises will *strengthen* your back.
The storm *strengthened* overnight.
The deal has *strengthened* their position.

gloss: To increase suddenly and strongly.
examples: Demand tends to *surge* before the holidays.
Applications *surged* after the ad ran.
Energy prices have been *surging* since May.

gloss: To rise very quickly to a high level.
examples: Rents could *soar* again next year.
Temperatures *soared* into the nineties.
The stock has been *soaring* all month.
contrast: *Soar* sounds exactly like *sore* (painful), but they are different words.

gloss: To raise something to a higher level, position, or quality.
examples: Good design can *elevate* an ordinary room.
The award *elevated* her to a new level of fame.
*Elevating* your leg will help with the swelling.

transitivity: both — transitive (accelerate the process), intransitive (the car accelerated)
gloss: To go faster or happen sooner, or to make something do so.
examples: The new plan should *accelerate* the process.
Hiring *accelerated* in the second half of the year.
Climate change is *accelerating*.

gloss: To make something as large or as effective as possible.
examples: We want to *maximize* the space in this room.
They *maximized* profits by cutting shipping costs.
He is *maximizing* his time at the gym.

gloss: To make something smaller in size, amount, or degree.
examples: The city hopes to *reduce* traffic downtown.
They *reduced* the price by half.
Waste has been *reduced* by a third.
contrast: *Reduce* something **to** a level, or **by** an amount: *reduced by half*.

transitivity: both — transitive (decrease the dose), intransitive (sales decreased)
gloss: To become less in number or amount, or to make something less.
examples: Sales usually *decrease* in January.
The number of accidents *decreased* last year.
Rainfall has been *decreasing* for a decade.
contrast: Verb: dih-KREES. Noun: DEE-krees.

gloss: To move something down, or to make an amount or level smaller.
examples: They agreed to *lower* the rent.
He *lowered* his voice so the baby would not wake up.
Interest rates are being *lowered* again.

transitivity: both — transitive (diminish someone's role), intransitive (the noise diminished)
gloss: To become smaller or less important, or to make something seem so.
examples: Nothing can *diminish* what she did that night.
His influence *diminished* over the years.
The pain has been *diminishing* since Friday.

transitivity: both — transitive (lessen the pain), intransitive (the pain lessened)
gloss: To become less, or to make something less.
examples: A hot drink may *lessen* the pain.
The risk *lessened* after the second dose.
The medicine is *lessening* the swelling.
contrast: *Lessen* (make less) sounds exactly like *lesson* (a class).

transitivity: both — transitive (shorten a video), intransitive (the days shorten)
gloss: To become shorter, or to make something shorter.
examples: Can you *shorten* the video to two minutes?
They *shortened* the workweek to four days.
The days are *shortening* already.

transitivity: both — transitive (narrow the list), intransitive (the road narrows)
gloss: To become less wide, or to reduce something to fewer choices.
examples: The road *narrows* past the bridge.
We *narrowed* the list to three names.
The gap has been *narrowing* since spring.

transitivity: both — transitive (weaken the wall), intransitive (the storm weakened)
gloss: To become less strong, or to make something less strong.
examples: Skipping meals will *weaken* you.
The storm *weakened* before it reached land.
The dollar has *weakened* against the euro.

gloss: To become gradually smaller or fewer until little is left.
examples: Supplies *dwindle* fast in a storm.
The crowd *dwindled* to about twenty people.
Our savings have been *dwindling* all year.

gloss: To become smaller, weaker, or worse over a period of time.
examples: Membership continues to *decline*.
Sales *declined* for the third quarter in a row.
His health has been *declining* since the fall.

gloss: To fall very fast and very far.
examples: Prices can *plummet* overnight.
The stock *plummeted* after the news.
Temperatures have been *plummeting* all week.
contrast: The stress is on the first syllable, so the *t* does not double: *plummeted*, *plummeting*.

transitivity: both — transitive (contract a muscle), intransitive (metal contracts)
gloss: To become smaller or shorter, especially by pulling in.
examples: Metal *contracts* as it cools.
The economy *contracted* for two quarters.
Her muscles were *contracting* in spasms.
contrast: Verb (get smaller): kuhn-TRAKT. Noun (an agreement): KAHN-trakt.

gloss: To reduce something to the smallest possible amount or degree.
examples: We want to *minimize* the risk.
They *minimized* delays by hiring more drivers.
He kept *minimizing* his own part in it.

gloss: To keep something below a certain amount, size, or number.
examples: Please *limit* your answer to one page.
They *limited* each customer to two boxes.
The budget is *limiting* what we can do.
contrast: The stress is on the first syllable, so no doubling: *limited*, *limiting*. *Limit* something **to** an amount.

gloss: To put a limit on what someone may do or on how much there can be.
examples: The city may *restrict* parking on this street.
The doctor *restricted* his salt intake.
Access has been *restricted* to staff.
contrast: *Restrict* something **to** a group or an amount.

gloss: To cut a small amount off something, or to reduce it slightly.
examples: We need to *trim* the budget.
He *trimmed* the hedge on Saturday.
They are *trimming* costs wherever they can.
contrast: One vowel plus one final consonant doubles: *trimmed*, *trimming*.

gloss: To use up most of the supply of something.
examples: A long winter can *deplete* the whole supply.
The drought *depleted* the reservoir.
Their savings have been *depleted* by medical bills.

transitivity: both — transitive (slow the traffic), intransitive (growth slowed)
gloss: To move or happen more slowly, or to make something do so.
examples: Rain will *slow* the traffic.
Growth *slowed* in the second half of the year.
The train was *slowing* as it came into the station.

transitivity: both — transitive (improve the road), intransitive (his English improved)
gloss: To become better, or to make something better.
examples: Your English will *improve* with practice.
They *improved* the road last summer.
Her scores have *improved* every month.

gloss: To increase the quality, value, or attractiveness of something.
examples: A little salt will *enhance* the flavor.
The lighting *enhanced* the photos.
They are *enhancing* the security of the app.

gloss: To improve something by making small changes to it.
examples: We can *refine* the plan next week.
She *refined* her technique over many years.
The model is being *refined* with new data.

gloss: To make something as good as it can possibly be.
examples: It takes years to *perfect* a recipe.
He *perfected* his accent by watching movies.
She has been *perfecting* the design for months.
contrast: Verb: pur-FEKT. The adjective (*a perfect day*) is PUR-fikt.

gloss: To make something work as well or as efficiently as possible.
examples: We can *optimize* the site for phones.
They *optimized* the route and saved an hour.
The team is *optimizing* the code this week.

gloss: To make a process simpler and more efficient.
examples: We should *streamline* the hiring process.
They *streamlined* the menu down to ten dishes.
The office is *streamlining* its paperwork.

gloss: To improve the quality or value of something by adding to it.
examples: Reading will *enrich* your vocabulary.
Compost *enriched* the soil.
The program has *enriched* the whole community.
contrast: The third person adds -es after -ch: *enriches*.

gloss: To fill something up again after it has been used.
examples: We need to *replenish* the supplies.
The rain *replenished* the reservoirs.
Shelves are being *replenished* every morning.

transitivity: both — transitive (worsen the pain), intransitive (the weather worsened)
gloss: To become worse, or to make something worse.
examples: Stress can *worsen* the symptoms.
The weather *worsened* in the afternoon.
Traffic has been *worsening* for years.

gloss: To become gradually worse in quality or condition.
examples: Bread will *deteriorate* quickly in this humidity.
His eyesight *deteriorated* after the illness.
Relations between the two sides have been *deteriorating*.
contrast: Five syllables, dih-TEER-ee-uh-rayt — do not drop the second *r*.

transitivity: both — transitive (sunlight degrades plastic), intransitive (the plastic degrades)
gloss: To reduce the quality or condition of something, or to break down over time.
examples: Sunlight can *degrade* plastic.
The tape *degraded* over thirty years in the attic.
The signal has *degraded* since the storm.

transitivity: both — transitive (the sun faded the curtains), intransitive (colors fade)
gloss: To lose color, strength, or clarity little by little.
examples: Bright colors *fade* in the sun.
The music *faded* as we walked away.
His memory of that day has *faded*.

gloss: To stop developing or improving.
examples: Wages can *stagnate* for years.
The project *stagnated* after the manager left.
The economy has been *stagnating* since 2022.

ru: восстанавливаться, идти вверх после падения; отскакивать
gloss: To recover and rise again after a fall or a setback.
examples: Markets usually *rebound* after a shock.
Sales *rebounded* in the fall.
The team has *rebounded* from a terrible start.
contrast: Verb: rih-BOWND. The noun (*on the rebound*) is REE-bownd.

transitivity: both — transitive (develop a product), intransitive (the story developed)
gloss: To grow or change into something more advanced, or to create something over time.

They *developed* the software in six months.
She is *developing* a new course for the fall.
contrast: The stress falls on -VEL-, so the *p* does not double: *developed*, *developing*.

gloss: To become fully grown, fully developed, or more sensible.

The cheese has been *maturing* for two years.

gloss: To move forward or develop toward a better or later stage.

The illness *progressed* more slowly than expected.
Work is *progressing* well on the new wing.

transitivity: both — transitive (advance a theory), intransitive (science advances)
gloss: To move forward, develop, or move up to a higher position.
examples: Technology continues to *advance*.

She has *advanced* to a senior position.

gloss: To grow strongly and do very well.
examples: Few plants *flourish* in this soil.

gloss: To produce flowers, or to develop into something better.
examples: The cherry trees *blossom* in April.
She *blossomed* into a confident speaker.
Their friendship has *blossomed* into something more.

gloss: To produce flowers, or to be at one's healthiest and best.

The garden *bloomed* early after the warm spring.
The desert was *blooming* after the rain.

gloss: To grow plants, or to develop a skill, quality, or relationship over time.

gloss: To care for something while it grows and to help it develop.

gloss: To start something meant to last, or to prove that something is true.

gloss: To start an organization, company, or town that is meant to continue.

gloss: To provide room for someone or something, or to change your plans to fit their needs.
examples: The hall can *accommodate* three hundred people.

We are *accommodating* two extra guests this weekend.

ru: настраивать под себя, делать на заказ
gloss: To change something so that it fits a particular person or purpose.
examples: You can *customize* the dashboard.

gloss: To adapt something so that it fits a particular need or person.

gloss: To change something so that it suits or belongs to one particular person.

gloss: To make things follow one single standard or pattern.
examples: The state wants to *standardize* the tests.
They *standardized* the parts across all models.
Forms are being *standardized* department by department.

gloss: To control something by rules, or to keep it at the right level.
examples: Agencies *regulate* what can go on a label.
The industry was barely *regulated* at the time.
The thermostat is *regulating* the temperature.

transitivity: both — transitive (moderate your tone), intransitive (the wind moderated)
gloss: To make something less extreme, or to become less extreme.
examples: Try to *moderate* your expectations.
He *moderated* his tone after the first question.
The heat has *moderated* since Sunday.
contrast: Verb: MAH-duh-rayt. The adjective (*moderate prices*) is MAH-duh-rit.

transitivity: both — transitive (stabilize the patient), intransitive (prices stabilized)
gloss: To stop changing and become steady, or to make something steady.
examples: The new tires *stabilize* the car in the rain.
Prices *stabilized* after the harvest.
His condition has *stabilized*.

gloss: To keep something steady, or to give two things equal weight.
examples: It is hard to *balance* work and school.
She *balanced* the tray on one hand.
The budget has been *balanced* for three years.

gloss: To make something easier to do or to understand.
examples: Let's *simplify* the form.
The new law *simplified* the whole process.
They are *simplifying* the instructions.
contrast: -y becomes -ie-: *simplifies*, *simplified*; *simplifying* keeps the y.

gloss: To make something more difficult or more confusing than it was.
examples: Let's not *complicate* things.
The delay *complicated* our travel plans.
Rain is *complicating* the repairs.

gloss: To change repeatedly up and down, or from one level to another.
examples: Gas prices *fluctuate* from week to week.
His weight *fluctuated* all winter.
The signal has been *fluctuating* since morning.

transitivity: both — transitive (alternate the shifts), intransitive (they alternated between two songs)
gloss: To happen or to do something in turns, one after the other.
examples: We *alternate* weekends at my mother's house.
They *alternated* between English and Spanish.
Sunny days have been *alternating* with storms.
contrast: Verb: AWL-tur-nayt. The adjective (*an alternate route*) is AWL-tur-nit.

gloss: To vary between two limits.
examples: Tickets *range* from twenty to eighty dollars.
The answers *ranged* from angry to funny.
We saw cars *ranging* from tiny hatchbacks to old pickups.
contrast: *Range* **from** one point **to** another.

transitivity: both — transitive (continue the story), intransitive (the rain continued)
gloss: To keep happening or to keep doing something without stopping.
examples: The talks will *continue* on Monday.
It *continued* to rain all afternoon.
She has *continued* working part time.

transitivity: both — transitive (cease operations), intransitive (the noise ceased)
gloss: To stop happening, or to stop doing something — a formal word for *stop*.
examples: The noise did not *cease* until midnight.
The company *ceased* operations in March.
Fighting has *ceased* along the border.

gloss: To begin again after a pause.
examples: We will *resume* right after lunch.
Play *resumed* once the rain stopped.
She has *resumed* her studies.
contrast: Verb: rih-ZOOM. The noun *résumé* (a CV) is REZ-uh-may.

gloss: To make something last longer.
examples: Nobody wants to *prolong* this meeting.
The treatment *prolonged* his life by years.
Arguing only *prolongs* the whole process.

gloss: To keep something going at the same level over time.
examples: The soil cannot *sustain* that many crops.
They *sustained* the pace for two hours.
Growth has been *sustained* for six quarters.

gloss: To keep something in the same condition or at the same level.
examples: It is hard to *maintain* that speed for long.
They *maintained* the building for forty years.
She has *maintained* her grades while working.

gloss: To keep something safe from harm, loss, or change.
examples: The town wants to *preserve* the old depot.
Cold air *preserved* the ice into May.
The letters have been *preserved* in a museum.

transitivity: both — transitive (merge the files), intransitive (the two roads merge)
gloss: To join together into one, or to join things into one.
examples: The two lanes *merge* after the light.
The banks *merged* last year.
They are *merging* the two departments.
contrast: *Merge* **with** another company, or **into** one lane.

transitivity: both — transitive (combine two offices), intransitive (the two gases combine)
gloss: To join two or more things so that they work or exist together.
examples: *Combine* the flour and the sugar in a bowl.
They *combined* the two offices into one.
The class *combines* history and art.
contrast: Verb: kuhm-BYN. The noun (a harvesting machine) is KAHM-byn.

ru: интегрировать, объединять; включаться в общую систему
transitivity: both — transitive (integrate the systems), intransitive (the app integrates with others)
gloss: To combine things into one working whole, or to become part of a group.
examples: The app can *integrate* with your calendar.
They *integrated* the new team in a month.
The schools were *integrated* in the 1960s.
contrast: *Integrate* **into** a system, or **with** another one.

transitivity: both — transitive (divide the work), intransitive (the road divides)
gloss: To separate something into parts, or to share it out.
examples: Let's *divide* the work evenly.
The river *divides* the town in two.
The class was *divided* into four groups.
contrast: *Divide* something **into** parts, or **between** two people.

gloss: To make an exact copy of something, or to repeat it exactly.
examples: Don't *duplicate* work someone has already done.
She *duplicated* the key at the hardware store.
The results have been *duplicated* by another lab.
contrast: Verb: DOO-pluh-kayt. The noun and adjective (*a duplicate key*) are DOO-pluh-kit.
